title: Optimal cosine measure, quantitative rigidity and local optimality for direct-sum positive bases
shortTitle: Best directions for derivative-free search: perpendicular simplices
oneLine: Among positive bases built from simplices in complementary subspaces, the cosine measure is at most 1/√(r₁² + … + rₖ²), reached only by perpendicular regular simplices; these configurations are also strict local optima among all configurations, a local form of a 2003 sphere-covering conjecture.
abstract: Direct-search methods minimise a function without derivatives by trying a fixed set of directions, and they work only if one direction always points roughly downhill. The cosine measure scores a set of unit directions by its worst case: the cosine of the largest angle between any direction and the nearest trial direction. Maximising it is the same as covering the sphere by equal caps of smallest radius. Hare, Jarry-Bolduc and Planiden (2023) asked whether, among positive bases that split into minimal positive bases of complementary subspaces, the best ones must have mutually orthogonal subspaces. This candidate proves that if the subspaces have dimensions r₁, …, rₖ the cosine measure is at most (r₁² + … + rₖ²)^(−1/2), with equality exactly for regular simplices in mutually orthogonal subspaces, answering the question in every dimension and size. Exact identities for the loss give quantitative rigidity, with a sharp stability exponent that changes from 1/2 to 1 at size ⌈3n/2⌉. Going beyond the class, every orthogonal union of regular simplices is a strict local maximiser of the cosine measure among all configurations of the same number of unit vectors, up to rotation: a local form of the Böröczky–Wintsche conjecture on optimal coverings by few caps, in every dimension. The argument extends to shifted blocks under a convex-hull condition, which an explicit example in four dimensions shows can fail. Limits: the global question remains open for sizes n + 3 to 2n − 2, the size of the neighbourhood is not quantified, and constants are not optimal. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: A 22-page paper with a plain introduction (the problem, positive bases, a table of what was known, what is new, a roadmap) and complete written proofs; the proofs are analytic and no step is computational. One Python script (NumPy and mpmath, fixed seed) makes 6301 explicit floating-point checks: the polar-vertex formula and the exact identities on 312 configurations in twelve block types, independent vertex enumeration for 72 small configurations, the sharpness examples, the four-dimensional shifted example (squared radius 27), the Section 7 variation formulas against 40-digit finite differences, and positive definiteness on the critical subspace for twelve types. A clean replay from fresh copies in normal and python -O mode reproduced the recorded output byte for byte, and a wrong coefficient makes the script fail.

keyResults: Theorem 3.1 (proof): for every direct sum of minimal positive bases of complementary subspaces of dimensions r₁, …, rₖ, cm(D) ≤ (r₁² + … + rₖ²)^(−1/2), with equality if and only if the subspaces are mutually orthogonal and every block is a regular simplex.

Corollary 3.2 (proof): the maximum over Ω_{n,s} is S_*^(−1/2) with S_* = (k − b)a² + b(a + 1)², attained exactly by balanced orthogonal regular simplices; Corollary 3.3 reduces both questions of Hare, Jarry-Bolduc and Planiden to whether optimal positive bases have zero critical vectors.

Theorem 5.2, Proposition 5.3 and Theorem 6.1 (proofs): exact loss identities control cross-block angles linearly and simplex shapes with a square-root rate; the optimal stability exponent is 1 when s ≥ ⌈3n/2⌉ and 1/2 otherwise.

Theorem 7.1 and Corollary 7.2 (proofs): every orthogonal union of regular unit simplices is a strict local maximiser of the cosine measure among all configurations of s unit vectors, up to rotation, with quadratic growth of the loss; so the configurations of the Böröczky–Wintsche conjecture are strict local optima for every dimension, and in R⁴ with six vectors the unbalanced type (3,1) (cm = 1/√10) is a local but not global maximum (optimum 1/√8).

Theorem 8.2 and Corollary 8.3 (proofs): the bound extends to shifted blocks whose shifts lie in the convex hull of the preceding vectors; Section 8.1 gives a positive basis of R⁴ with cm⁻² = 27 for which this condition fails for every decomposition.

narration: Optimal directions for searching without derivatives: an Evidence Press briefing. Some optimisation methods cannot use derivatives. Instead they try a small, fixed set of directions from the current point, and move if one of them helps. That only works if, whatever the downhill direction is, one of the trial directions points roughly the same way. The cosine measure scores a set of directions by its worst case: the cosine of the largest angle between any direction in space and the nearest trial direction. Bigger is better. The same number answers a question in geometry: how small can equal caps be, centred on those directions, and still cover the whole sphere? Two geometers, Böröczky and Wintsche, conjectured which few caps cover the sphere best. Split the dimensions into nearly equal groups, put a regular simplex, such as a triangle or a tetrahedron, in each group, and set the groups at right angles to each other. Hare, Jarry-Bolduc and Planiden asked a related question about positive bases built from simplices in complementary subspaces: must the best ones sit at right angles? This candidate proves that, within that class, they must, in every dimension and for every size. The cosine measure is at most one over the square root of the sum of the squared group dimensions, and only perpendicular regular simplices reach that bound. Arrangements that come close to the best are nearly perpendicular and nearly regular, at an exact rate. Going further, the perpendicular arrangement cannot be improved by any small change of the directions, even a change that leaves the structured class. So the conjectured best coverings are at least locally best, in every dimension. There is a twist. In four dimensions with six directions, a tetrahedron beside a perpendicular pair is also a local optimum, although two perpendicular triangles do better, so a local search can get stuck there. The proof picks a random corner of a related polytope and compares the farthest corner with the average. The paper credits this device to public figures by Jarry-Bolduc and Krishan Lal, who drew it for triangles and pairs. The global question for most sizes stays open, and the local result does not say how large the safe neighbourhood is. Evidence Press published this anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, and its review was internal, not peer review. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Hare, Jarry-Bolduc and Planiden (2023), Nicely structured positive bases with maximal cosine measure. Optimization Letters. The question answered here for every dimension and size (Theorem 3.1); the optimum over orthogonal structures (their Theorem 33, Corollary 34) and the case of five vectors in three dimensions (Proposition 30, Theorem 31).
Nævdal (2019), Positive bases with maximal cosine measure. Optimization Letters. The optimal minimal and maximal positive bases, recovered here in one argument.

Hare, Jarry-Bolduc, Kerleau and Royer (2024), Using orthogonally structured positive bases for constructing positive k-spanning sets with cosine measure guarantees. Linear Algebra and its Applications. Orthogonally structured positive bases.
Hare and Sun (2026), On the computation of cosine measures in high dimensions. EURO Journal on Computational Optimization. The cosine measure computed through the polar polytope (their Theorem 3.2).

Böröczky and Wintsche (2003), Covering the sphere by equal spherical balls. Discrete and Computational Geometry (Algorithms and Combinatorics). Conjecture 1.3 on optimal coverings by few equal caps, proved here in local form (Corollary 7.2), and Theorem 1.4 on coverings by d + 3 caps.
Litvak, Sonnleitner and Szczepanski (2026), Minimal dispersion on the sphere. Discrete & Computational Geometry. Restates the balanced-simplex covering conjecture.
Borodachov (2022), Optimal antipodal configuration of 2d points on a sphere in R^d for covering. arXiv:2210.12472. The best antipodal coverings by 2d points.

decisionObject.description: Treat perpendicular regular simplices as the optimal direct-sum positive bases (cm = (r₁² + … + rₖ²)^(−1/2)), and as strict local optima among all configurations of the same size, when choosing poll directions for direct search or candidate sphere coverings by few caps.
decisionObject.scope: Direct sums of minimal positive bases for the global statement; a neighbourhood of unspecified size for the local statement; the global question over all positive bases and coverings remains open for n + 3 ≤ s ≤ 2n − 2.
